Experiments that changed questions

Six degrees of separation: it's a small world

Milgram asked for letters to reach a stranger in Boston passing only through acquaintances. Those that arrived used about five intermediaries.

As well as his famous obedience study, Stanley Milgram investigated in 1967 how small the world is. He gave people in Nebraska and Kansas a letter addressed to a stranger in Boston. If they did not know him, they were to send it to an acquaintance they thought was closer to him, and so on.

What arrived

Many letters got lost along the way. But those that arrived did so, on average, after passing through about five or six people. That popularised the phrase "six degrees of separation", which became the title of a play and a film.

Later studies using email confirmed similar figures, and in 2016 Facebook calculated that any two users are on average about three and a half degrees apart. Short chains do not mean they are easy to find: many of Milgram's letters ended up in someone's drawer.

References

  1. Travers, J. y Milgram, S. (1969). An experimental study of the small world problem. Sociometry, 32(4), 425–443.
  2. Dodds, P. S., Muhamad, R. y Watts, D. J. (2003). An experimental study of search in global social networks. Science, 301(5634), 827–829.
